title: Problem Overview
content:
**Erdős Problem #607: Incidence Signatures of Point Configurations**

For $n$ points $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$, the incidence signature $A = \{|\ell \cap P|\}$ records point counts per line. $F(n)$ counts distinct achievable signatures.

**Solved**: $F(n) = \exp(\Theta(\sqrt{n}))$ (Szemerédi-Trotter). Prize: \$250.
mathContext: The problem connects the Szemerédi-Trotter incidence theorem ($I \leq O((nm)^{2/3} + n + m)$) to a counting problem. The $\sqrt{n}$ growth arises from the Hardy-Ramanujan partition function: signatures correspond to constrained partitions of $\binom{n}{2}$.

title: Point
content: **Point** = `EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)` — a point in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with the standard Euclidean metric.
mathContext: The Mathlib `EuclideanSpace` provides the inner product structure needed for collinearity checks. Points are vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2$ with componentwise operations.

title: PointConfig
content:
**PointConfig n**: a configuration of $n$ labeled, distinct points in $\mathbb{R}^2$.
- `points : Fin n → Point` — indexed point map
- `distinct : Function.Injective points` — no coincident points

Distinctness ensures every pair determines a well-defined line.
mathContext: The distinctness condition is essential: coincident points would collapse lines and artificially simplify signatures. The labeling by $\text{Fin}\, n$ allows us to use Finset combinatorics.

title: Line
content:
**Line**: a line in $\mathbb{R}^2$ determined by two distinct points (`point1 ≠ point2`).

The `ne` field proves the defining points are distinct, ensuring the line is well-defined (not a degenerate 'point').
mathContext: Lines are the fundamental objects in incidence geometry. Two points determine a unique line; three or more points on the same line create collinearities that affect the incidence signature.

title: Line.contains
content:
**Line.contains l p**: point $p$ lies on line $l$ iff $p = p_1 + t(p_2 - p_1)$ for some $t \in \mathbb{R}$.

This is the parametric form: $t=0$ gives $p_1$, $t=1$ gives $p_2$, and other values give other points on the line.
mathContext: The parametric representation avoids issues with vertical lines that the slope-intercept form $y = mx + b$ would face. It naturally extends to higher dimensions and is compatible with the vector space structure of `EuclideanSpace`.

title: Line Through a Pair
content: **lineThroughPair p q h**: the unique line determined by two distinct points $p \neq q$. Each unordered pair of distinct configuration points determines exactly one such line, and the multiset of incidence counts over all these determined lines is the configuration’s incidence signature.
mathContext: Two distinct points $p, q \in \mathbb{R}^2$ lie on a unique line $\{p + t(q-p) : t \in \mathbb{R}\}$. An $n$-point configuration determines at most $\binom{n}{2}$ such lines (fewer when several points are collinear, since one line then absorbs many pairs).

title: incidenceCount
content:
**incidenceCount config l**: counts configuration points lying on line $l$.

$|\ell \cap P| = |\{i \in \text{Fin}\, n : \ell.\text{contains}(P_i)\}|$

For a determined line, always $2 \leq |\ell \cap P| \leq n$.
mathContext: The incidence count is the fundamental measure in the Szemerédi-Trotter theorem. The total number of incidences $I = \sum_\ell |\ell \cap P|$ is bounded by $O((nm)^{2/3} + n + m)$ where $m$ is the number of lines.

title: incidenceSignature
content:
**incidenceSignature config**: the `Multiset ℕ` of incidence counts for all determined lines.
$$A = \{|\ell_1 \cap P|, |\ell_2 \cap P|, \ldots, |\ell_m \cap P|\}$$

This captures the full collinearity structure of the configuration.
mathContext: The multiset retains multiplicities: if 5 lines each contain 3 points, the count 3 appears 5 times. The SET form `incidenceSet` ignores multiplicities. The problem asks about the set form $A$ (which values appear), not the multiset (how often each value appears).

title: F(n)
content:
**F n**: the number of distinct incidence signatures achievable by $n$-point configurations in $\mathbb{R}^2$.

$F(n) = |\{\text{incidenceSignature}(P) : P \text{ is an } n\text{-point configuration}\}|$

Despite infinitely many configurations, $F(n)$ is finite (and surprisingly small).
mathContext: The finiteness of $F(n)$ is non-obvious: there are uncountably many $n$-point configurations, but the incidence signature can only take finitely many values because each count is in $\{2, \ldots, n\}$ and there are at most $\binom{n}{2}$ lines.

title: Pair-Counting Constraint
content: **incidence_pair_constraint**: each unordered pair of distinct points determines exactly one line, so $\sum_i \binom{k_i}{2} = \binom{n}{2}$ where the $k_i$ are the incidence counts. This forces every incidence signature to be a constrained integer partition of $\binom{n}{2}$ — the combinatorial heart of the problem.
mathContext: Writing $m_i = \binom{k_i}{2} \ge 1$, the identity $\sum_i m_i = \binom{n}{2} \approx n^2/2$ realizes the signature as a partition of $\binom{n}{2}$ into triangular-number parts. $F(n)$ counts only the geometrically realizable such partitions.

title: Upper Bound: F(n) ≤ exp(C√n)
content: **sz_trotter_upper_bound**: $F(n) \le \exp(C\sqrt{n})$ for an absolute constant $C>0$. This is the Szemerédi–Trotter (1983) resolution of Erdős #607 (the $250 prize): the incidence bound limits which partitions of $\binom{n}{2}$ are geometrically realizable, and Hardy–Ramanujan partition asymptotics cap their number at $\exp(O(\sqrt n))$.
mathContext: The Szemerédi–Trotter incidence theorem $I(P,L) \le C(nm)^{2/3}+n+m$ restricts realizable incidence signatures; the count of admissible partitions of $\binom{n}{2}$ is $\exp(O(\sqrt n))$, yielding the upper bound.

title: incidence_at_least_two
content:
**incidence_at_least_two**: Every determined line contains $\geq 2$ configuration points.

This is immediate: the line is determined by a pair of points, both of which lie on it.
mathContext: The lower bound $|\ell \cap P| \geq 2$ means incidence counts live in $\{2, 3, \ldots, n\}$, not $\{0, 1, \ldots, n\}$. This constraint reduces the space of possible signatures.

title: incidence_at_most_n
content:
**incidence_at_most_n**: Every line contains $\leq n$ configuration points (trivially).

Equality $|\ell \cap P| = n$ holds only for collinear configurations where all points lie on one line.
mathContext: The upper bound $n$ is achieved by the collinear configuration, which has signature $A = \{n\}$. This is one extreme; the other is general position with $A = \{2\}$.

title: Lower Bound: F(n) ≥ exp(c√n)
content: **f_lower_bound**: $F(n) \ge \exp(c\sqrt n)$ for some $c>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$. Explicit point sets (e.g. arithmetic-progression configurations) realize $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt n))$ distinct signatures, matching the upper bound and proving $F(n) = \exp(\Theta(\sqrt n))$.
mathContext: Unconstrained partitions of $n$ into parts of size $2..n$ already number $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt n))$ (Hardy–Ramanujan), and geometric constructions realize enough of them to give the matching lower bound.

title: Small Value: F(2) = 1
content: **F_two**: $F(2)=1$. Two distinct points determine exactly one line containing both, so the only achievable incidence signature is $\{2\}$.
mathContext: With $n=2$ there is a single determined line with incidence count $2$, hence one signature $\{2\}$ and $F(2)=1$. This is the base case anchoring the counting function.

title: Small Value: F(3) = 2
content: **F_three**: $F(3)=2$. Three points are either collinear — one line, signature $\{3\}$ — or in general position — three lines, signature $\{2,2,2\}$. These are the only two cases, so $F(3)=2$.
mathContext: Collinear triple $\Rightarrow$ one line meeting all $3$ points, signature $\{3\}$; non-collinear (general position) $\Rightarrow$ three lines each meeting exactly $2$ points, signature $\{2,2,2\}$. Two realizable signatures give $F(3)=2$.

title: Related Problems and Grid Tightness
content: Erdős #607 sits beside #606 (counting achievable numbers of determined lines), #101 (maximum point–line incidences — exactly Szemerédi–Trotter), and #102 (bichromatic incidences). Square grid configurations are the canonical tight examples for the Szemerédi–Trotter bound.
mathContext: An $m\times m$ grid has $n=m^2$ points and achieves $\Theta((nm)^{2/3})$ incidences, certifying tightness of the Szemerédi–Trotter theorem and underpinning the $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt n))$ lower bound for $F(n)$.

title: szemeredi_trotter_incidence
content:
**szemeredi_trotter_incidence**: The famous Szemerédi-Trotter theorem (1983):

$$I(P,L) \leq C \cdot (nm)^{2/3} + n + m$$

where $I$ counts point-line incidences, $n = |P|$, $m = |L|$.
mathContext: This is one of the most important results in combinatorial geometry. The proof uses the crossing number inequality: any graph drawn in the plane with $v$ vertices and $e > 4v$ edges has $\geq e^3/(64v^2)$ crossings. Applying this to the incidence graph yields the $O((nm)^{2/3})$ bound. Alternative proofs use polynomial partitioning (Guth-Katz 2015).

title: Partition Connection
content:
**Why $\sqrt{n}$?** Incidence signatures encode constrained integer partitions.

If lines have incidences $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_m$, then $\sum_i \binom{k_i}{2} = \binom{n}{2}$ (each pair of points determines one line).

The number of such partitions grows as $\exp(\Theta(\sqrt{n}))$ by the Hardy-Ramanujan asymptotic.
mathContext: Hardy and Ramanujan (1918) proved $p(n) \sim \frac{1}{4n\sqrt{3}} \exp\left(\pi\sqrt{\frac{2n}{3}}\right)$. Here we're partitioning $\binom{n}{2} \approx n^2/2$ into parts $\binom{k_i}{2}$, but the geometric constraints (Szemerédi-Trotter) reduce the effective partition count from $\exp(O(n))$ to $\exp(O(\sqrt{n}))$.

title: erdos_607
content:
**erdos_607**: The complete solution combining both bounds:
$$\exp(c\sqrt{n}) \leq F(n) \leq \exp(C\sqrt{n})$$

Proved by `⟨szemeredi_trotter_607, lower_bound_construction⟩`.
mathContext: This gives a tight characterization of $F(n)$ up to constants in the exponent. The upper bound uses the Szemerédi-Trotter incidence theorem; the lower bound uses explicit constructions. The problem is completely resolved: $F(n) = \exp(\Theta(\sqrt{n}))$.

title: erdos_607_tight
content:
**erdos_607_tight**: Restates the tight asymptotic with explicit existential constants:

$\exists c, C$ with $0 < c < C$ such that eventually $\exp(c\sqrt{n}) \leq F(n) \leq \exp(C\sqrt{n})$.

Defined as `partition_count_growth`.
mathContext: The exact values of $c$ and $C$ are not determined by the formalization. Finding them is listed as an open question. The gap between $c$ and $C$ reflects the difference between the best known constructions and the best known upper bound.
